Biological materials, such as bamboo, are naturally optimized composites with
exceptional mechanical properties. Inspired by such natural composites, tra-
ditional methods involve extracting nanoﬁbers from natural sources and
applying them in composite materials, which, however, often results in less
ideal mechanical properties. To address this, this study develops a bottom-up
nanoﬁber assembly strategy to create strong ﬁber-reinforced composite
hydrogels inspired by the hierarchical assembly of bamboo. Self-assembled
chitosan-sodium alginate nanoﬁbers (CSNFs) are combined with tannic
acid (TA) and poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) as the interfacial crosslinker and
hydrogel matrix, respectively, to emulate the fundamental cellulose-lignin-
hemicellulose composition unit of bamboo. Strong interfacial electrostatic
interactions and hydrogen bonding form between the functional groups of
these components. These molecular interactions can be further reinforced by
constructing higher-order structure through stretch-induced orientation. The
resulting composite hydrogel achieves good mechanical performance,
including a high tensile strength of up to 60.2 MPa and a simultaneous high
strength of 48.0 MPa and ultimate strain of 470%. This approach demonstrates
a hierarchical bottom-up strategy to construct strong and robust composite
hydrogels by effectively leveraging fundamental molecular interactions. By
mimicking bamboo’s highly integrated structural composition, it offers a
promising solution for creating advanced bioinspired materials with excellent
mechanical properties.
Almost all natural materials are composites, often featuring highly
organized strength-providing ﬁbers, networks, or platelets embedded
in heterogenous toughness-enhancing matrices, and arranged in
hierarchical
structures
to
optimize
mechanical
properties
and
functionality1–3. Notably, bamboo is lightweight, strong, and ﬂexible,
combining typically contradictory mechanical properties4. Bamboo
features a hierarchical ﬁbrous structure fundamentally composed of
cellulose, lignin, and hemicellulose (Fig. 1a, b). In this combination,
crystalline cellulose microﬁbrils act as the reinforcing elements to
provide strength within plant cell walls; lignin ﬁlls the spaces between
cellulose ﬁbers, offering stiffness and resistance to deformation; and
hemicellulose serves as a cohesive matrix that binds cellulose and
lignin together to enhance ﬂexibility5,6. Their excellent chemical
compatibility ensures effective bonding and load transfer, distributing
stress evenly and preventing localized failures. Despite being a het-
erogeneous composite, bamboo exempliﬁes a synergistically inte-
grated structural material, with hierarchical structures assembled from
the fundamental cellulose-lignin-hemicellulose composition unit.
Inspired by these natural composites, compositing has become a
classic material design approach for enhancing various materials,

including soft materials like hydrogels7. Polysaccharide-based ﬁbers
such as cellulose, commonly extracted from lignocellulosic plants,
have attracted wide interest as reinforcing materials in composites for
their natural origin, biocompatibility, and high mechanical properties,
with natural cellulose ﬁbers exhibiting a tensile strength up to 1.6–3
GPa8. However, traditional top-down processes to extract cellulose
from natural sources typically involve complex mechanical and che-
mical treatments, which can easily damage the interfaces of the
nanoﬁbers. According to Ito et al., etching can cause atomic-scale
dents on the extracted cellulose nanoﬁbers, resulting in defects and
thus inferior mechanical properties in the ﬁnal composites9. In addi-
tion, the excessively high modulus of natural cellulose nanoﬁbers,
ranging from 20–50 GPa due to its high degree of crystallization10,
differs signiﬁcantly from most hydrogel matrices. This mismatch can
lead to undesirable stress concentration within the composite system,
compromising its mechanical properties11–13. Despite signiﬁcant efforts
made to extract cellulose nanoﬁbers from natural sources, the incor-
poration of these ﬁbers often results in material combinations and
mechanical properties inferior to their natural counterparts. Since the
original natural sources of cellulose, such as bamboo, already exhibit
well-integrated material compositions, a potentially more effective
approach would be to directly mimic their compositional and struc-
tural organizations using a bottom-up approach.
To directly mimic bamboo’s hierarchical assembly from its fun-
damental composition unit using a bottom-up approach, it is essential
to achieve synergistic interactions between three components: the
ﬁbers, the matrix, and their interfaces. We propose using an
ultrasonication-assisted
molecular
assembly
process
to
create
polysaccharide-based nanoﬁbers from components such as chitosan
and sodium alginate, instead of the traditional top-down extraction
method14.

nanoﬁbers,

making them ideal for reinforcing hydrogels.Additionally, their defect-
free microstructure and functional interfaces allow them to interact
with other molecules to form the matrix and interfaces necessary for
constructing the fundamental composition units. Speciﬁcally, we
propose combining these nanoﬁbers with tannic acid (TA) and poly(-
vinyl alcohol) (PVA) to mimic bamboo’s cellulose-lignin-hemicellulose
unit, with TA acting as a strong lignin-like crosslinker and PVA serving
as a ﬂexible hydrogel matrix similar to hemicellulose. By assembling
these fundamental units, we can create higher-order lamellar struc-
tures that replicate bamboo’s hierarchical organization. This bottom-
up approach enables the development of composite hydrogels that
closely resemble bamboo’s highly integrated structural composition
with the potential to achieve enhanced mechanical performance.
Herein, a bottom-up nanoﬁber assembly strategy is developed to
construct strong ﬁber-reinforced composite hydrogels from bamboo-
inspired
fundamental
composition
units.
In
this
strategy,
polysaccharide-based nanoﬁbers are combined with TA and PVA to
form the fundamental composition unit with strong molecular inter-
actions. Moreover, these interactions can be effectively coordinated
and reinforced through subsequent stretch-induced orientation15. The
resulting bamboo-inspired composite hydrogel exhibits excellent
mechanical performance, including a high tensile strength up to
60.2 MPa. In addition, a high strength of 48.0 MPa and ultimate strain
of 470% can be simultaneously achieved, thanks to the synergistic
effects of the aligned structure and molecular interactions in the fun-
damental composition units of the composite hydrogel. Inspired by
the composition unit of bamboo, this work proposes a hierarchical
bottom-up approach to constructing strong and robust ﬁber-
reinforced composite hydrogels based on the most fundamental
molecular interactions.
Results
Bamboo-inspired design of the fundamental composition unit
As illustrated in Fig. 1a, bamboo exhibits a hierarchical structure that
extends from its macroscopic hollow tube conﬁguration to the
microscale organization of vascular bundles, and further down to the
integration of cellulose ﬁbrils within a hemicellulose-lignin matrix. This
hierarchical structure, including the vascular bundles and cellulose
ﬁbrils, are strategically aligned along the length of bamboo to optimize
its mechanical performance. Its fundamental composition unit of cel-
lulose, lignin, and hemicellulose is essential for constructing higher-
order structures that can effectively enhance the mechanical proper-
ties. Within this unit, strong molecular interactions exist as covalent
bonds between lignin and hemicellulose, and hydrogen bonds
between lignin and hemicellulose, as well as between cellulose and
hemicellulose (Fig. 1b). These molecular interactions are key to the
synergistic integration of the components.
Inspired by the hierarchical assembly of bamboo, this study
developed a fabrication strategy for ﬁber-reinforced composite
hydrogels by constructing fundamental composition units and form-
ing higher-order structures to leverage their intrinsic strength (Fig. 1c).
Similar to the cellulose ﬁbrils in bamboo, polysaccharide-based
nanoﬁbers were prepared through an ultrasonication-induced assem-
bly process (Supplementary Fig. 1). In this approach, chitosan and
sodium alginate macromolecules were oriented and assembled under
a high-energy acoustic ﬂow ﬁeld. Strong electrostatic interactions
between the oppositely charged groups of the two polysaccharides led
to the formation of chitosan-sodium alginate nanoﬁbers (CSNFs,
Supplementary Fig. 2a). These nanoﬁbers featured inherently func-
tional surfaces with characteristic groups of chitosan and sodium
alginate, including amino (–NH2) and hydroxyl (–OH) groups. These
functional groups served as important starting points to design the
molecular interactions within the fundamental composition units. In
this study, PVA and TA, both rich in –OH groups, were used as the
hydrogel matrix and crosslinker, respectively. To prepare the CSNF-
TA-PVA hydrogel, CSNFs were ﬁrst mixed with a PVA solution, and the
mixture was casted and dried. Then, the material was rehydrated in a
TA solution, allowing TA to inﬁltrate and crosslink the composite. The
–OH groups of TA could potentially form molecular interactions with
the –NH2 groups of CSNFs and the –OH groups of PVA (Fig. 1c).
To preliminarily validate the above composition unit design, the
mechanical properties of pure PVA (pure hydrogel matrix), CSNF-
PVA (ﬁber-reinforced hydrogel matrix), and CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogels
(ﬁber-reinforced hydrogel matrix with interfacial reinforcement)
were compared in Fig. 2a. After air drying and rehydration (in deio-
nized water), the pure PVA hydrogel exhibited a tensile strength of
4.6 MPa and an ultimate strain of 360%. Upon the incorporation
of ﬁbers at ratios ranging from 1:20 to 1:5 (CSNF-to-PVA), the strength
of the composite hydrogels was effectively enhanced (Supplemen-
tary Fig. 2b). However, at an excessively high ﬁber content of 1:1,
CSNF-PVA became more rigid with lower tensile strength. A 1:10 ratio
was selected for further experiments, as it offered a balanced com-
bination of enhanced mechanical properties and a swelling ratio of
2.8, close to the PVA swelling ratio of 2.9 (Supplementary Fig. 2c). At
this ratio, the CSNF-PVA hydrogel demonstrated a tensile strength of
9.5 MPa and an ultimate strain of 480%, achieving a well-balanced
improvement in strength and stretchability. After introducing TA in
CSNF-PVA hydrogel, the obtained CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel achieved
the highest tensile strength of 13.8 MPa (three times that of the pure
PVA hydrogel and 2.2 times that of the PVA-TA hydrogel) and an
ultimate strain of 500%.
Meanwhile, cyclic loading-unloading tensile tests were performed
to evaluate the energy dissipation behavior of the hydrogels (Supple-
mentary Fig. 2d, e). The results indicated that both the tensile stress
and energy loss coefﬁcient increased with the addition of CSNF and
TA. Speciﬁcally, the energy loss coefﬁcients of CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel
in the ﬁrst and tenth cycles were measured to be 0.86 and 0.58,
respectively, which were signiﬁcantly higher than those observed for
the PVA and CSNF-PVA hydrogels. The hydrogen bonding between
CSNF, TA, and PVA promoted effective stress transfer and energy
absorption, improving energy dissipation throughout the material.
While most composite hydrogels see increases in stiffness and
strength at the expense of stretchability, the incorporation of CSNF
and TA in the PVA hydrogel improved all three properties, highlighting
the effectiveness of the material composition design. In the CSNF-PVA
hydrogel, the elastic and amorphous CSNFs were highly compatible
with the PVA matrix in mechanical and chemical properties. Both
featuring –OH groups, their integration could form abundant hydro-
gen bonds, leading to simultaneous improvements in strength and
stretchability. Moreover, the addition of TA further strengthened the
matrix and enhanced the ﬁber-matrix interfaces by providing more
–OH groups as functionalsites, which ultimately resulted in the highest
mechanicalperformance of the CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel. The synergy of
the three components was also conﬁrmed by atomic force microscopy
(AFM), where the CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel exhibited a homogeneous
and robust structure with a higher modulus than the pure PVA
hydrogel (Supplementary Fig. 3).
Molecular interactions within the fundamental
composition unit
The speciﬁc molecular interactions within the CSNF-TA-PVA compo-
sition unit were carefully studied. As shown in Fig. 2b and Supple-
mentary Fig. 4a, b, the N1s spectrum of CSNF-PVA exhibited a peak at
400.0 eV, corresponding to the –NH2 group of the amino side chain. In
contrast, the N 1 s spectrum of CSNF-TA-PVA revealed two character-
istic peaks at400.0 eV and 401.9 eV, corresponding to –NH2 and –NH3
+
groups, respectively. This indicated that in addition to the hydrogen
bonds between the phenolic –OH groups of TA and the –NH2 groups of
CSNF, the weakly acidic TA could also release phenoxy anions to form
electrostatic interactions with the –NH3
+ groups of CSNF.

Meanwhile, the phenolic –OH groups of TA were also supposed to
form hydrogen bonds with PVA. To validate this, Fig. 2c and Supple-
mentary Fig. 4c compared the FTIR spectra of TA, PVA, CSNF-PVA, and
CSNF-TA-PVA. The C = O vibration of TA shifted from 1697 cm−1 to
1708 cm−1 in CSNF-TA-PVA, indicating strengthened vibrational energy
of the C = O bonding due to interaction with the hydrogen donor16,17. In
addition, the peaks at 1170 cm−1 and 1308 cm−1, which corresponded to
the asymmetrical stretch of aromatic C–O, slightly shifted to 1187 cm−1
and 1315 cm−1, respectively. The peak of C–O–C stretch also shifted
from 1007 cm−1 to 1021 cm−1. Notably, the broadening of the hydroxyl
stretching vibration at 3258 cm−1 in CSNF-TA-PVA (Supplementary
Fig. 4d) indicated the formation of a greater number of new, dis-
ordered hydrogen bonds. This broadening effect was indicative of
increased hydrogen bond heterogeneity and was attributed to the
incorporation of TA, which disrupted the existing hydrogen bonding
network in PVA, while forming additional, non-uniform hydrogen
bonding interactions. These XPS and FTIR results revealed the
favourable binding capacity of TA with both CSNF and PVA, which was
mostly driven by secondary interactions including hydrogen bonding,
van der Waals forces, and CH-π interactions18.
The changes of molecular environment in composite hydrogel
were also revealed using Raman spectroscopic analysis. As shown in
Supplementary Fig. 4e, the decrease in intensity of the stretching
vibration of –CH (1441 cm−1) in CSNF-TA-PVA and stretching vibrations
of –CH2 (2914 cm−1) in the Raman spectrum were strong indicators of
reduced crystallinity in PVA. These peaks in PVA appeared sharp and
well-deﬁned, reﬂecting the ordered and regular packing of polymer
chains. As the crystallinity decreased, the molecular arrangement
became more disordered, leading to a broadening of these peaks. This
transformation indicated a disruption of the regular packing of PVA
chains, leading to a higher proportion of amorphous content. Addi-
tionally, the intensity peak of C = O stretching vibrations (1712 cm−1)
decreased, suggesting alterations in the molecular environment (the
formation of strong hydrogen bonds), further supporting the disrup-
tion of regular PVA packing and the enhanced hydrogen bonding
network facilitated by TA.

To further validate the above observed molecular interactions
and understand their forming mechanisms, density functional theory
(DFT) calculations were performed to determine the binding energies
of TA with CSNF and PVA. The calculations were conducted using the
B3LYP/6-311 G(d, p) basis set. A chitosan molecule was selected to
represent the surface of CSNF, and the polyphenol side chain of TA was
used as its representative unit. The optimized structures and calcu-
lated electrostatic potential (ESP) distributions of the units were pre-
sented in Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 5.
On the one hand, TA could readily bond with the –NH3
+ and –NH2
groups of CSNF through electrostatic interactions and hydrogen
bonding, respectively. The ESP maps of TA and CSNF units indicated
strong electrostatic interaction, with attractive potential concentrated
on the phenoxy oxygen atom of TA (117.3 kcal/mol) and the hydrogen
atom of the amino cation of CSNF (−141.8 kcal/mol, Supplementary
Fig. 6 and Table 1). The binding energy of this interaction was up to
−27.9 kcal/mol (Supplementary Fig. 7). Additionally, the binding
energy between neutral CSNF and TA was calculated as −17.7 kcal/mol
(Fig. 2e and Supplementary Table 2), indicating a very strong hydrogen
bond. On the other hand, the negatively charged oxygen atoms of TA
formed hydrogen bonds with the positively charged hydrogen atoms
of PVA, with the binding energy between TA and PVA calculated to be
−13.0 kcal/mol (Fig. 2f). Notably, the hydrogen bonding of TA with
both CSNF and PVA exhibited higher binding energies than that
between the –OH groups of PVA molecules themselves, which was only
−8.3 kcal/mol (Fig. 2g). These calculations conﬁrmed the above mole-
cular characterizations and validated the proposed molecular inter-
action design within the CSNF-TA-PVA composition unit. Upon the
addition of TA, it ﬁrst bonded with CSNFs through electrostatic
interactions and hydrogen bonding, and then with PVA through
hydrogen bonding. In this process, TA functioned as the hydrogen
bond acceptor to connect CSNF and PVA, with the hydrogen atom in
the latter two as the donor. These molecular interactions well
integrated the three components into a synergistic whole, thereby
enhancing the overall mechanical properties of the composite
hydrogel.
Evolution of the nanocrystalline structure
In the pure PVA hydrogel, the hydrogen bonds between PVA molecules
are integral to the formation of nanocrystalline domains that con-
tribute to the mechanical properties19,20. As the incorporation of TA
induced stronger hydrogen bonds within the PVA matrix, its effect on
the nanocrystalline structure was studied.
As shown by the differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) results in
Fig. 3a, the pure PVA hydrogel exhibited a crystallization peak at 225 °C
(i.e., the melting temperature Tm21), while CSNF-PVA showed a lower
Tm at 220 °C. The introduction of the CSNF disrupted the ordered
structure of PVA, leading to a reduction in crystallinity. This structural
disruption resulted in a shift of Tm to lower temperatures. Further-
more, as the bonds between PVA molecules were replaced by stronger
hydrogen bonds formed between TA and PVA, the increased number
of strong hydrogen bonds caused further destruction of crystalline
regions and a reduction in the thermal stability of molecular chains,
which resulted in the lowest Tm at 213 °C22 in the CSNF-TA-PVA
hydrogel. This shift conﬁrmed the above DFT calculations that TA-PVA
hydrogen bonds were stronger than PVA-PVA hydrogen bonds, dis-
placing PVA crystalline domains due to competitive effects.
Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) was carried out to understand
the evolution of PVA crystallization. As presented in Fig. 3b, c, PVA
crystallization peaks were observed in the PVA and CSNF-PVA hydro-
gels at 0.064 Å−1 and 0.07 Å−1, respectively. However, no peak was
identiﬁed for the CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel due to the reconﬁguration of
its internal interactions. Using the critical vector corresponding to the
peak intensity qmax, the average distance between crystalline domains
was estimated by the Bragg expression L = 2π/qmax, with results
summarized in Supplementary Table 3. The average distance in the

To further quantify the evolution of the crystalline morphology,
X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurement was performed. The pure PVA
hydrogel revealed a strong diffraction peak at 2θ = 19.7° (Fig. 3d), cor-
responding to the typical reﬂection plane of (101) semicrystalline PVA24.
The introduction of TA caused a signiﬁcant reduction in the PVA crys-
tallization peak, showing that the strong hydrogen bonds between TA
and PVA inhibited the crystallization of PVA chains. The size of crystal-
line domains was approximately evaluated by the Scherrer’s equation
D = kλ/(β cos θ)25, where D is the average size of crystalline domains, β is
the full-width half maximum, k is a dimensionless shape factor varying
with the actual shape of the crystalline domain (set as 1), λ is the
wavelength of X-ray diffraction, and θ is the Bragg angle. The detailed
data are summarized in Fig. 3e and Supplementary Table 3. The average
size of crystalline domains decreased signiﬁcantly from 3.29 nm to
1.14 nm with the addition of CSNF and TA. This decrease in the size of
PVA crystalline domains was consistent with the SAXS results, where the
PVA crystallization peak was negligible for the CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel.
These results indicated that the strong interactions between
CSNF, TA, and PVA predominated over the hydrogen bonds between
PVA molecules. The hydrogen bonds between TA and PVA molecules
formed while breaking the hydrogen bonds between PVA chains,
reducing the size of PVA crystalline domains and the average distance
between them.
Biomimetic higher-order aligned structure of composite
hydrogels
Bamboo’s mechanical properties stem from its hierarchical structure.
Cellulose nanoﬁbers, hemicellulose, and lignin are integrated within
the cell wall as the fundamental components. The cells are aligned
along the bamboo’s length, forming microscale arrangement of vas-
cular bundles. The overall wall structure, combined with the precise
alignment of these components, is essential for distributing mechan-
ical stresses and maintaining the structural integrity of bamboo. As the
above results revealed the characteristics and effects of the strong
molecular interactions within the bamboo-inspired CSNF-TA-PVA
composition unit, the next step was to investigate whether these
interactions could be leveraged to construct higher-order structures
that would further enhance the mechanical properties, in a similar
manner as bamboo’s hierarchical assembly.
The CSNF/PVA-TA hydrogel was post-treated by stretch-induced
orientation in its microstructure. After being stretched to twice its
length and air dried, the hydrogel was reswollen and ﬁxed in a sodium
sulfate solution, which could harden the molecules and preserve the
orientation.
The SEM images in Fig. 4a–c revealed the microstructure of the
aligned CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel. It exhibited a highly oriented structure
with stress-induced parallel wrinkles throughout the sample on the
macro scale (Fig. 4a). On the meso scale, a homogeneous lamellar
structure was observed owing to the air drying process (Fig. 4b). No
clear boundaries between the different components could be
observed, indicating that the components were well-integrated into a
synergistic composite through the intricate design of molecular
interactions. As such, only ﬁber bundles could be deliberately sepa-
rated from the composite hydrogel on the micro scale (Fig. 4c). These
ﬁber bundles were formed by the aggregation of multiple aligned
fundamental composition units.
Additionally, two-dimensional (2D) SAXS tests were conducted to
quantitatively evaluate the orientation. An elliptical scattering ring
pattern was observed in the aligned CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel (Fig. 4d).
After azimuthal angle analysis on the 2D SAXS results, the aligned
CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel exhibited a Herman’s orientation factor fc of
0.64, indicating a highly anisotropic structure (Fig. 4e). Meanwhile, no
signiﬁcant changes by FTIR, XRD, and SAXS analyses in the interactions
or crystalline structures in the composite hydrogel before and after
ﬁxing in the sodium sulfate solution (Supplementary Fig. 8a–c).
Therefore, the salt treatment primarily inﬂuenced the density of the
crosslinked network without modifying the existing molecular inter-
actions or crystalline regions within the composite hydrogel.
As shown in Fig. 4f, the aligned CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel revealed a
high tensile strength of 48.0 MPa, with an ultimate strain of 470%.
Notably, the strength was 4 times that of the unaligned composite
hydrogel, with only a minimal reduction in stretchability. This sug-
gested that the high degree of orientation not only aligned the CSNFs
but also brought the functional groups of CSNF, TA, and PVA mole-
cules closer together with this aligned arrangement, increasing
hydrogen bonds at their interfaces. These combined effects enabled
the hydrogel to sustain higher stress while maintaining its stretch-
ability. In comparison, both aligned CSNF-PVA and aligned PVA-TA
hydrogels showed lower mechanical properties than those of the
aligned CSNF-TA-PVA (Supplementary Fig. 8d). Speciﬁcally, the
aligned CSNF-PVA hydrogel achieved a tensile stress of 40.0 MPa and
an ultimate strain of 296%, while the aligned PVA-TA hydrogel had a
tensile stress of 29.7 MPa and an ultimate strain of 278%. These ﬁndings
demonstrated the synergistic effects of the enhanced interactions
between the composite units. In addition, when ﬁxed in a higher-
concentration salt solution after stretching, the strength of the aligned
CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel could reach up to 60.2 MPa (with a strain of
250%) by excessively hardening the hydrogel (Supplementary Fig. 8e).
The hydrogel displayed signiﬁcant anisotropy, exhibiting a strength of
19.5 MPa and an elongation at break of 670% in the direction perpen-
dicular to its orientation.
Figure 4g summarized the gradual improvements in strength by
ﬁrst assembling the fundamental CSNF-TA-PVA composition units and
an even more drastic increase by arranging them into aligned struc-
tures. The overall signiﬁcant mechanical enhancement highlighted the
effectiveness of the proposed design inspired by the hierarchical
assembly of bamboo. As a result, the aligned CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel
stood out from other reported PVA hydrogels in the literature with a
combination of high strength and good stretchability (Fig. 4h and
Supplementary Table 4). These excellent mechanical properties could
extend the potential applications of hydrogels in mechanically
demanding scenarios. As demonstrated in Fig. 4i, a small piece of the
composite hydrogel could lift heavy objects up to 20 kg (50,000 times
its own weight) without breaking.
Synergistic strengthening and toughing mechanisms through
strong molecular interactions
Compared to the pure PVA hydrogel, the aligned CSNF-TA-PVA com-
posite hydrogel demonstrated signiﬁcant improvements in stiffness,
strength, and stretchability (Fig. 5a). As a result, its toughness, calcu-
lated as the total mechanical energy absorbed, increased about 20
times from 6.24 MJ/m3 in the pure PVA hydrogel up to 122.4 MJ/m3
(Fig. 5b and Supplementary Table 5). Meanwhile, a fracture toughness
was calculated to be 14.3 MJ/m3 (Supplementary Fig. 8f). To under-
stand the synergistic strength and toughness enhancements, the
effects of the micro, nano, and molecular characteristics of the
oriented composite hydrogel were investigated.
On the micro scale, the fracture surfaces of different hydrogels
were analyzed (Supplementary Fig. 9). While the pure PVA hydrogel
exhibited a smooth, straight fracture, uneven fracture surfaces were
observed in both CSNF-PVA and aligned CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogels. The
incorporation of CSNFs as a heterogenous reinforcement phase could
hinder and deﬂect fast crack propagation in the PVA matrix. In

interaction design.
On the nano scale, the crystalline structure of the aligned CSNF-
TA-PVA hydrogel under stretching was characterized using in-situ
wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) tests (Fig. 5c). Minimal increases in
the PVA crystallization peak (marked by the arrow) were observed
under continuous tensile load, indicating that tensile stress barely
induced PVA crystallization. This again conﬁrmed previous results that
stronger TA-PVA hydrogen bonds substituted PVA-PVA hydrogen
bonds. Therefore, these micro and nano characterizations highlighted
the crucial role of molecular interactions between CSNF, TA, and PVA
in mechanical enhancement.
As illustrated in Fig. 5d, the fundamental CSNF-TA-PVA composi-
tion units featured multiple molecular bonds, primarily hydrogen
bonds and electrostatic interactions. The hydrogen bonds mainly
existed at the CSNF-TA and TA-PVA interfaces, with original PVA-PVA
hydrogen bonds outcompeted by TA-PVA bonds due to higher binding
energy (Supplementary Fig. 10). Meanwhile, stronger electrostatic
interactions also formed between CSNF and TA, as well as between
chitosan and sodium alginate in forming the CSNFs. The combined
effects of these interactions contributed to the hydrogel’s strength and
toughness. The TA-PVA hydrogen bonds not only replaced weaker
PVA-PVA bonds but also created additional binding sites, increasing
the overall bonding density and strength of the PVA matrix. Mean-
while, the electrostatic interactions on the CSNFs formed a robust
framework that resisted deformation and distributed stress evenly
across the hydrogel. These molecular interactions are well evidenced
by the measurements and DFT calculations. Furthermore, the nano-
crystalline structure are replaced by the networks formed by the three
components owing to the stronger interactions. On the micro scale,
the strong interactions signiﬁcantly reinforce the interlayer bonding
within the material, thereby enhancing the toughness of the hydrogel
through effective energy dissipation. The subsequent orientation
process further ampliﬁes the interfacial interactions, leading to an
overall improvement in the mechanical properties of the material. This
synergistic interplay of hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions
operates across hierarchical levels, enabling the bamboo-inspired
hydrogel to sustain high mechanical loads while maintaining ﬂexibility.

Hence, the excellent mechanical properties of the aligned CSNF-TA-
PVA hydrogel rooted on the bamboo-inspired fundamental composi-
tion units and their intricately engineered molecular interactions.
Building on the mentioned multiscale synergistic reinforcement,
our bamboo-inspired hydrogel exhibited excellent impact resistance
and energy absorption capabilities, as evidenced by the dynamic
mechanical tests performed using the Split-Hopkinson Pressure Bar
(SHPB) (Fig. 6a). Upon impact, the hydrogel exhibited a strong resis-
tance force and effectively absorbed the impact energy. The maximum
compressive stress of the aligned CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel reached
148.2 MPa (Fig. 6b) under high-strain-rate compression (6000 s−1),
exceeding the performance of conventional hydrogels (Fig. 6c)26–30.
The energy absorption during compression was measured as 36.3 MJ
m−3 at the strain rate of 6000 s−1. A pronounced strain rate sensitivity
indicated that the aligned CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel can effectively
accommodate varying impact velocities through multiple energy dis-
sipation mechanisms. The layered structure as the structural frame-
works resisted the shock stress. At larger strains, the deformation
progressed to the microscale polymer network and ultimately
involved nanoscale shear behavior at the CSNF-TA-PVA interfaces,
further contributing to energy dissipation and impact resistance. The
falling-ball impact test demonstrated that the hydrogel possessed
excellent impact resistance. As shown in Fig. 6d, the glass plate pro-
tected by the hydrogel remained intact upon the impact of a steel ball.
This capability highlighted its potential for applications in harsh
mechanical environments, providing a robust protective layer under
demanding conditions. By overcoming the inherently poor mechanical
strength of hydrogels, this work laid the groundwork for broader
applications across various ﬁelds, such as ﬂexible electronics, biome-
dical devices, energy storage devices, and soft robotics.
Discussion
In summary, this study developed a bottom-up nanoﬁber assembly
strategy inspired by the hierarchical organization of bamboo. Self-
assembled
polysaccharide-based
nanoﬁbers,
with
compatible
mechanical properties and inherently functional surfaces, were com-
bined with TA as the interfacial crosslinker and PVA as the hydrogel
matrix to form the fundamental composition unit. Detailed molecular
and nanoscale characterizations revealed strong interfacial electro-
static interactions and hydrogen bonding between the components,
which overpowered and broke down the original nanocrystalline
structure within the PVA matrix. Compared to the pure PVA hydrogel,
the CSNF-TA-PVA composite hydrogel demonstrated simultaneous
enhancements in both strength and stretchability, increasing from 4.6
to 13.8 MPa and from 360% to 500%, respectively. Moreover, upon
stretch-induced
orientation,
the
strength
further
increased
to
48.0 MPa with an ultimate strain of 470%, and the highest strength of
60.2 MPa was achieved. This mechanical improvement showcased a
similar principle found in bamboo, where the intrinsic strength of the
fundamental composition units was effectively leveraged and opti-
mized by the oriented high-order structure. The synergistic effects of
interfacial electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonds enabled the
bamboo-inspired composite hydrogels to sustain high mechanical
loads while maintaining ﬂexibility. Hence, this study presented a model

Materials

Preparation of chitosan-sodium alginate nanoﬁbers (CSNF)
A 2 wt% CS solution was prepared by dissolving 1.0 g of CS in 49 g of
acetic acid solution (1 wt% in deionized water). A 2 wt% SA solution was
prepared by dissolving 1.0 g of SA in 49 g of deionized water. 50 g of
the CS solution and 50 g of the SA solution were mixed in a 1:1 ratio.
The mixture was then ultrasonicated for 2 h using an ultrasonic
homogenizer (JY92-IIDN, 900 W, 25 kHz, Ningbo Scientz Biotechnol-
ogy Co., Ltd.) to obtain a chitosan-sodium alginate nanoﬁber (CSNF)
suspension.
Preparation of the CSNF-TA-PVA composite hydrogel
A 10 wt% PVA solution wasprepared by dissolving 10 g of PVA in 90 g of
deionized water. The CSNF-PVA mixture was obtained by mixing the
CSNF suspension and PVA solution together in a 1:10 mass ratio. Then,
the mixture was degassed and casted in a petri dish (diameter: 90 mm)
and dried in air to obtain the CSNF-PVA composite. The CSNF-TA-PVA
hydrogel was obtained by reswelling the dried CSNF-PVA composite in
a 30 wt% TA solution for two days. For comparison, the pure PVA and
CSNF-PVA hydrogels were obtained by immersing dried PVA and
CSNF-PVA composite in deionized water for 2 days. The PVA-TA
hydrogel was obtained by immersing the dried PVA in TA solution
(30 wt%) for 2 days.
Preparation of the aligned CSNF-TA-PVA composite hydrogel
The PVA-TA-CSNF hydrogel was stretched to 100% strain and main-
tained while air drying. After completely dried, the composite was
ﬁxed and re-swollen in a sodium sulfate solution (20 ~ 30 wt%). The
swelling ratios of all samples were determined by the swelling volume
ratio Qv = Vswollen/V0, where Vswollen and V0 represented the equilibra-
tion volume of hydrogels after soaking in solution and their initial
volume in the dry state, respectively.

ning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) with Hitachi Regulus 8230 and
Hitachi S4800. X-ray diffraction tests were performed using a Bruker
D8 diffractometer. The zeta potential was measured with a Malvern
Zetasizer Nano ZS90. The AFM images were captured in tapping mode
using a Bruker MultiMode 8 scanning probe microscope (SPM,
VEECO). Phase images were obtained using a piezo response force
microscope (PFM, MFP-3D, Asylum Research, Oxford, UK). Fourier
transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) spectra were characterized
using an ATR-FTIR, Agilent CARY 660. Raman analysis was conducted
using a confocal Raman microscope (Alpha300R, WITec GmbH)
equipped with a TEM single-frequency laser (λ = 532 nm, laser
power = 40 mW). DSC was employed to characterize the melting and
crystallization properties.X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was

excitation source.

Mechanical test
The mechanical properties were measured on a universal tester
Instron 5500 with a 1000 N load cell at a constant loading speed of
1 mm/s. The hydrogel samples were cut into the dog-bone shape
(length: 15 mm, width: 2 mm, and thickness: 0.30 mm) for the uni-
axial tensile test. The toughness was deﬁned as the amount of energy
absorbed before fracture and calculated as the integral area under
the tensile stress-strain proﬁle. The cyclic load-unload tensile test
was performed at a constant loading speed of 2 mm/s (with a max-
imum strain of 150%). The energy loss coefﬁcient (η) was calculated
using the formula: η = Wloss/Winput, where Wloss was the energy dis-
sipated and Winput was the total energy input during the loading
phase. Unnotched and single-notched gel samples (with a pre-cut
notch with a length of one-third of the sample width) were tested to
evaluate fracture toughness. Notched samples were stretched until
crack propagation occurs, and the critical strain (εc) was recorded.
The fracture toughness was determined by integrating the stress-
strain curve of the unnotched sample from zero up to the critical
strain (εc) obtained from the notched sample.
Split-Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) experiments
The SHPB apparatus used in this study included a strike bar, incident
bar, transmission bar, absorber bar, and a data acquisition system. The
strike bar was accelerated by the release of compressed air. When the
strike bar impacted the incident bar, it produced an elastic compres-
sive wave that propagated through the specimen. The data acquisition
system then captured the incident, reﬂected, and transmitted pulses,
which were subsequently analyzed to determine the mechanical
properties of the material.

Falling-Ball impact testing of hydrogels
To evaluate the protective properties of hydrogel, the prepared
hydrogels were placed on a glass slide as a protective layer. A steel ball
weighing 32 g was dropped freely from a ﬁxed height of 1.5 m, directly
impacting the hydrogel-covered glass slide. The test was conducted to
assess the hydrogels’ ability to absorb impact energy and protect
the glass.
X-ray scattering measurement
Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) tests were performed using Xeuss
3.0 with a windowless Eiger2 R 1 M Dectris hybrid pixel silicon sensor.
The sample-detector distance was 500 mm. The X-ray energy utilized
was 30 W with a wavelength of 1.54 Å. The exposure time was set as
600 s. For in-situ wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) measurements,
the aligned CSNF-TA-PVA hydrogel at 0 %, 50 %, and 150% strain was
tested, with a sample-detector distance of 70 mm. The 2D SAXS and
WAXS images were processed with corrections by FIT2D. The azi-
muthal angle intensity distributions curves were analyzed by FIT2D
software. The degree of orientation was evaluated by the Herman’s
orientation parameter (fc)31.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations
DFT calculations were performed using the Gaussian 16 (Revision A.03)
computational package and GaussView 632. B3LYP functional33 and the
basis set 6–311 g(d,p)34 were performed for geometry optimizations,
energy calculations and frequency calculations via counterpoise Basis
Set Superposition Error corrections35 and the D3-version of Grimme’s
empirical dispersion correction36. A conductor-like polarizable con-
tinuum solvation model (CPCM) of water and an ultraﬁne integration
grid were applied. All geometries were optimized to a minimum, and
frequency calculations were performed at the same level of theory to
verify the absence of imaginary frequencies. The electrostatic poten-
tial (ESP) distribution of each atom was calculated by Multiwfn37,38. The
visualization of optimized structures and composites was processed
with VESTA 339.
